docs.title: Files
docs.text: An entry links to its files (the PDF, supplementary material...) in its file field. The files usually live in the files directory of the library (the filesdir setting), named after the name template (see Renaming files and keys), but an entry can link to a file anywhere.

docs.title: What add does with a file
docs.text:
The files setting says what papers add does with the PDF it adds, with the files of the entries of an added bibtex (papers add other.bib), with the files of an added folder (papers add --recursive DIR) and with the files attached with --attach:

files the file is placed in the files directory the original is removed move (default) yes, under its template name yes copy yes, as a hard link when possible (same file system), otherwise a copy no link no: the entry links to the file where it is no

Set it for a library with papers config files copy, or for all libraries of the user with papers config --global files copy. The options --move, --copy and --link of papers add override it for one command; -r/--rename is the same as --move, and -c the same as --copy.

A file that belongs to another library, i.e. a file inside the files directory of a library whose configuration (.papersconfig.json) is found in the file's directory or above, is never moved: in move mode it is copied instead (a hard link when possible), so that the other library keeps its link. The same holds for a file in the files directory of the pool of the library (see Pools). A file already in the files directory of the current library is renamed in copy mode too, rather than copied next to itself. A file downloaded by papers (a URL given to add or --attach) is always moved into the files directory.

In a library that is not local (local: false, the default), the files directory where add, file attach and file rename place the files is that of the pool, and the name template is the pool's (see Local or not).

docs.title: papers file
docs.text:
The commands of papers file act on the files of the entries. Those that take entries accept keys, DOIs, arXiv identifiers or ISBNs (see Naming entries), and - to read them from the standard input, one per line:

Command Action papers file rename [KEY...] place the files of the entries (all without KEY) in the files directory, under their template name; --keep-source keeps the originals too (hard links when possible) papers file mv SRC... DEST move files or folders, and update the links of the entries (below) papers file attach KEY FILE... attach files to an existing entry, following the files setting (--move, --copy, --link override it); the files the entry already has are not touched papers file detach FILE... [--key KEY...] remove the links to the files from every entry that links to them (only from the entries of --key with --key); the files are kept (below) papers file detach --key KEY... remove all the links of the entries papers file detach --broken [--key KEY...] remove the broken links (of all entries without --key) papers file rm FILE... [-r] [--key KEY...] remove the links to the files, then delete the files, like git rm (below) papers file check [KEY...] report broken links, files linked twice, identical files (same checksum) of an entry, and with --metadata a DOI of the PDF that differs from the DOI of the entry (this parses the PDFs) papers file clean remove the files of the files directory and its subfolders that no entry links to, asking for each one (-y/--yes does not ask)

papers file attach KEY FILE... is the low-level form of papers add FILE --doi DOI for an entry already in the library: when the DOI is that of a library entry, add attaches the file to it in the same way, without fetching anything (see Adding entries).

papers file check changes nothing unless --fix is passed. --fix only applies the repairs that cannot lose anything: paths saved by Mendeley (missing leading /, latex symbols such as {\_}) are repaired when the repaired path exists, and the second link to the same file, or to an identical file, is removed from the entry (the file itself stays on disk; papers file clean removes it). A broken link to a file of a pool (the pool renamed the file) is replaced by the pool entry's current file. Other broken links are reported, and removed with papers file detach --broken.

papers file clean skips hidden files and folders (such as .git) and .bib files. A folder of the layout of versions before 2.19 (with a hidden .<name>.bib) is removed as a whole when no entry links to its files.

docs.title: Moving files
docs.text:
papers file mv works like mv, with the rules of git mv, and updates the links of every entry that links to a moved file (links are compared by real path, so a link through a symbolic link is found too):

  1. a source file that no entry links to is an error;
  2. a source folder must contain at least one linked file; the whole folder moves, files that no entry links to included;
  3. with several sources, the destination must be an existing folder;
  4. a destination that exists as a file is an error, unless -f/--force (papers warns when entries link to the replaced file: their links then lead to the moved file);
  5. -n/--dry-run shows the moves and the links that change, and does nothing;
  6. moving the files directory of the library (or a folder that contains it) also updates the filesdir setting.

All checks run before anything moves: if one fails, nothing is moved. If a move fails midway (e.g. disk full), the bibtex is saved with the links of the files already moved, and the error is reported. The parent folders of the destination are created when needed. A folder that contains the bibtex or the library configuration cannot be moved with papers file mv.

papers file mv files/2013 files/archive/2013
papers file mv files ~/Documents/library-files    # also sets filesdir
papers file mv -n files/a.pdf files/b.pdf files/new/

Links from other libraries to the moved files break: papers cannot know about them.

docs.title: Detaching and removing files
docs.text:
A file can be linked from several entries: the chapters of a book that share the PDF of the volume, two papers that share a supplement. papers file detach FILE... removes the links to FILE from all of them and prints which entries lost a link. Links are compared by real path, so a broken link can be named too. The files stay on disk: papers file detach never deletes a file.

papers file rm FILE... works like git rm: it removes the links to FILE from every entry that links to it, then deletes the file.

  • A FILE that no entry links to is an error, and nothing changes (with --key: that none of the entries of --key links to).
  • -r FOLDER removes the linked files inside FOLDER (and its subfolders). Files that no entry links to stay where they are; the folders left empty are removed, FOLDER included, except the files directory of the library. Without -r, a folder is an error. papers file detach -r FOLDER removes the links in the same way, without deleting anything.
  • With --key, only the links of those entries are removed; a file that another entry still links to is kept on disk, and papers says so.
  • A file of the pool is never deleted (e.g. the files that a library that is not local links to): only the link is removed, and papers says so.
  • papers does not ask: the file was named on the command line. --dry-run shows the links that would be removed and the files and folders that would be deleted.

-k/--key takes one or more entries (keys, DOIs, arXiv identifiers or ISBNs), and can be repeated: --key K1 K2 is --key K1 --key K2; - reads them from the standard input. As it takes several values, write the files before it: in papers file rm --key K1 file.pdf, file.pdf would be read as an entry, and papers stops with the error file.pdf is not an entry: put the files before --key.

papers file detach files/volume.pdf                    # from all the chapters
papers file detach files/volume.pdf --key smith2020    # from one chapter
papers file detach --key smith2020                     # all its links
papers file rm files/old-version.pdf
papers file rm -r files/2013 --dry-run
papers list --tag draft -K | papers file detach --broken --key -

docs.title: Removing entries and their files
docs.text:
papers rm KEY... (or papers list ... --delete) removes entries. Their files that no remaining entry links to may be deleted too:

  • in a terminal, papers lists those that are inside the files directory and asks once whether to delete them (default: no);
  • --delete-files deletes them without asking, and also those outside the files directory; --keep-files keeps them without asking;
  • without a terminal (e.g. the keys come from a pipe), the files are kept, and papers lists them: papers file clean deletes them later;
  • a file outside the files directory is deleted only with --delete-files.

A file still linked from another entry is never deleted, nor a file in the files directory of the pool of the library (e.g. the files that a library that is not local links to, see Local or not). A file that is a hard link (e.g. to the file of another library) can be deleted: this only removes this link, and papers says so.

docs.title: Deprecated forms
docs.text: papers filecheck still works in v3, with a warning, and runs the corresponding commands: --rename (-c) is papers file rename (--keep-source), --delete-broken is papers file detach --broken, --hash-check and --fix-mendeley are papers file check --fix, --metadata-check is papers file check --metadata, and --clean-filesdir (--force) is papers file clean (--yes). The file actions of papers list are deprecated too (see Listing and searching), and so is papers add --attachment (now --attach; -a FILE attaches the file until v4, with a warning: -a is --author, see Adding entries).

docs.title: Git-tracked library
docs.text:
By default (when a git binary is available), a library created with papers init git-tracks any change to the bibtex file. Pass --no-git to opt out, and --git-lfs to also back up the attached files (see below):

$> papers init --bibtex papers.bib --filesdir files [ --no-git | --git-lfs ]

Libraries made by older papers versions keep their saved setting; run papers config git true (or papers config git-lfs true) to enable git-tracking on an existing library.

From now on, every change to the library will result in an automatic git commit. And the papers git ... command will work just as git ... executed from the backup directory. E.g. papers git remote add origin *REMOTE URL*; papers git lfs track files; papers git add files; papers git push. When git fails, it prints its own error message, and papers exits with git's exit code.

Under the hood, every save commits a copy of the bibtex file to the backup repository, with the files .papers/origin.bib (origin copies of the entries taken from the pool, see Pools) and .papers/distinct.json (pairs that are not the same paper) when they exist. If --git-lfs is passed, the attached files are backed up along with the bibtex: they are hard-linked into the backup directory and tracked with git-lfs, together with a copy of the bibtex whose file paths point into the backup (so the backup is self-contained). Background in issue 51. Since the copy in the backup directory is a hard link, a file edited in place in the library is also edited there until the next save commits it. papers restore, undo and redo first reset the backup directory to the committed snapshot, so they restore the committed version of the files (git writes a new file, and the library file is left as it is).

Backup occurs in a subfolder of ~/.local/share/papers/backups, whatever the location of the library. Type papers status -v to find out, or papers backup list to see every backup directory papers knows of and which library each belongs to. Orphaned directories (e.g. whose library was deleted) can be cleaned up with papers backup remove NAME (glob patterns allowed; asks before deleting unless -y/--yes is passed; -f/--force is the deprecated form).

Backup directories are named after the bibtex file and its parent folder, plus a hash of the full path (e.g. myproject-references-3f9a1c2b), so two libraries can never share a directory and same-named libraries remain recognizable. The library configuration stores the name of its backup directory, which each machine looks up in its own backup folder; only a backup directory outside that folder is stored as an absolute path. Each directory also contains a manifest.json recording the bibtex file it backs up; if a backup operation finds a directory that belongs to another library (which could happen with directories created by papers versions that used the bibtex name alone), it moves the current library to a fresh directory instead of mixing the two histories. Directories created by older versions keep their name and are adopted as-is.

The libraries of papers 2.2 to 2.4 kept their backup in .papers/ next to the bibtex, the folder of origin.bib and distinct.json since papers 3: the first backup moves that repository (its history and the files it tracks) to a new subfolder of the backup folder, with a warning, and the library configuration records it. A backup commit that fails (e.g. refused by a git hook) is a warning; the bibliography is saved anyway.

For libraries that are already in a git repository, the feature remains useful as it is the basis for papers undo and papers redo (see Undo and redo).

docs.title: Install papers
docs.text:
pip install papers-cli

Note there is another project registered on PyPI as papers, hence papers-cli for command-line-interface. The installed command is still papers.

docs.title: Name clash with GNOME Papers
docs.text:
The GNOME Papers document viewer (the default viewer on recent GNOME desktops) also installs a papers command; with both installed, whichever comes first in $PATH wins. Two mitigations are built in:

  • The package also installs the command under the unambiguous name papers-cli — call that, or set a shell alias (e.g. alias papers=papers-cli), on systems where the names collide.
  • Because this command may mask GNOME Papers, a call whose arguments are all existing files (paths or file:// URIs, as passed by file managers through the viewer's desktop entry) is handed over unchanged to the next papers executable in $PATH that is not this tool, i.e. GNOME Papers itself. Double-clicking a PDF and papers somefile.pdf therefore keep opening the viewer. If no other papers is found, the files are opened with the system's default viewer (xdg-open) instead; should that lead back to this command, it stops with an error rather than looping. Subcommand names always take precedence (papers ./list opens a file named list; papers list lists your library), and any flag disables the hand-over — call the viewer's binary directly for viewer-specific flags.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
• python 3.11+
  • PyMuPDF (preferred) or poppler-utils (only pdftotext and pdfinfo; deprecated): convert PDF to text for parsing
  • bibtexparser: parse bibtex files
  • scholarly: interface for google scholar
  • rapidfuzz: calculate score to sort crossref requests
  • unidecode: replace unicode with ascii equivalent

The Python dependencies are installed automatically with pip.

docs.title: Move library to a new location
docs.text:
Moving a library can be tricky. Simple cases are:

  • files are stored in a central repository, and the bibtex contains absolute paths. Then moving the bibtex by hand is fine.
  • files are stored alongside the bibtex, and the bibtex contains relative paths. Just move around the folder containing bibtex and files.

In any other cases, you risk breaking the file links.

Papers tries to be as little opinionated as possible about how files are organized, and so it relies on your own judgement and use case. When loading a bibtex, it always interprets relative file links as being relative to the bibtex file. When saving a bibtex, it will save file links according to the paths setting of the library (relative to the bibtex by default, see Configuration).

To move the files directory, or some of its files, use papers file mv: it updates the links of the entries, and the filesdir setting when the files directory itself moves (see Files):

papers file mv files ../shared/files

The following set of commands also works, provided the initial file links are valid (optional parameters in brackets):

touch new.bib
papers add /path/to/old.bib --bib new.bib [ --copy | --link ] [ --filesdir newfilesdir ]
rm -f /path/to/old.bib

By default the files of old.bib are moved into the files directory (--copy keeps them in place too, --link links to them where they are), except the files inside the files directory of another library, which are copied.

docs.title: Duplicates
docs.text:
It's easy to end up with duplicates in your bibtex. After adding PDFs, or every once in a while, do:

papers check --duplicates

It groups the entries that are the same paper, by the rule of papers add (same DOI, arXiv id, ISBN of two books, or else same authors and title; see Adding entries), and merges each group into one entry. A group never holds two entries with different DOIs: a copy without DOI that matches both goes with one of them, and the other comes up on the next check if it is still a match.

Entry 1 of a group, the target, is the entry with most fields. The merge works as in papers add: the target keeps its key, fields missing in it are added, the file links are kept. The other entries are removed, and their keys are added to the biblatex ids field of the target, so that \cite commands with the old keys keep working with biblatex (BibTeX ignores the field). Commands that take a KEY also accept a key of the ids field.

$> papers check --duplicates
Same paper: 2 entries (same title and authors)
  1  smith2020climate  article  doi 10.1000/abc123  files/smith.pdf
  2  Smith_2020        article  no doi              other/smith-preprint.pdf

@article{smith2020climate,
!  key      = smith2020climate
!             2: Smith_2020 (kept in ids)
   author   = {Smith, John and Doe, Jane}
   doi      = {10.1000/abc123}
+  file     = {files/smith.pdf;other/smith-preprint.pdf}
+  ids      = {Smith_2020}
!  journal  = {Nature}
!             2: {Nature Climate Change}
   keywords = {climate, mine}
   title    = {Climate sensitivity revisited}
   year     = {2020}
}
1 conflict. Entry 2 is removed after the merge; its key goes to ids.
  1 keep values of 1   2 take values of 2   f field by field   e edit
  t N make entry N the target   n not the same paper   s skip   q quit   ? help
>>> 1
merged into smith2020climate: Smith_2020 (kept in ids)

The answers are those of the dialogue of papers add (see Adding entries), with one more: t N makes entry N the target, so that its key is kept. n (not the same paper) leaves the entries as they are and records them in .papers/distinct.json, so that the next check does not ask again. A group whose entries differ only by key and file links is merged without a question.

--on-duplicate sets what to do with each group without asking:

Value What happens ask the dialogue (default when the standard input is a terminal) keep merge; conflicts keep the value of entry 1 skip leave the groups as they are (the default with -y/--yes) error exit with status 1 if there is any group, and list them (default without a terminal)

Groups that the title guard asks about (same DOI, but different entry types and titles) are never merged with keep.

To only see the groups, use papers list --duplicates (see Listing).

The -m/--mode option of earlier versions still works, with a warning: -m i is --on-duplicate ask, -m m is keep, -m s is skip. To remove entries, use papers rm.

docs.title: Checking and fixing files
docs.text:
papers file check reports broken links, files linked twice, identical files and, with --metadata, DOIs of PDFs that differ from their entry's DOI. It changes nothing unless --fix is passed, which applies the safe repairs only. Broken links are removed with papers file detach --broken:

papers file check
papers file check --fix
papers file detach --broken

papers file rename places the files in the files directory under their template name (see Renaming files and keys).

papers file clean removes the files of the files directory (and its subfolders) that no entry links to:

papers file clean

It asks before removing anything, unless -y/--yes is passed. It ignores hidden files and folders and .bib files; a folder with a .{folder}.bib file inside, which is how versions before 2.19 stored entries with several files (see Renaming files and keys), is removed as a whole when no entry links to its files. That command works best when the files are in their own folder, and not mixed up with other things, obviously.

papers file clean --dry-run --yes lists the files that no entry links to, without removing them: a way to check what is actually tracked and what is not.

See Files for all the papers file commands. papers filecheck is the deprecated form of these commands (it still works, with a warning).

docs.title: Listing and searching
docs.text: papers list is a powerful command, inspired by unix's find and grep. It lets you search your bibtex, output the result in a number of formats, or perform actions on the matched entries.

docs.title: Basic listing
docs.text:
Pretty listing by default (otherwise pass --plain for plain bibtex):

$> papers list
Perrette2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1)

docs.title: Search with keywords
docs.text:
Search with any number of keywords:

$> papers list perrette scaling approach sea level
... (short list)
$> papers list perrette scaling approach sea level --any
... (long list)
$> papers list --key perrette2013 --author perrette --year 2013 --title scaling approach sea level
... (precise list)

With --invert, papers list lists the entries that the same command without --invert does not list.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Tags are the keywords field of the entries (comma-separated). papers tag lists them with the number of entries, adds and removes them:

$> papers tag perrette2013 --add sea-level projections
$> papers tag
sea-level (12)
projections (3)
$> papers tag perrette2013 --rm projections
$> papers tag --rename sea-level sea-level-rise     # in the whole library
$> papers list --tag sea-level projections
Perrette2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1, sea-level | projections )

papers list ... --add-tag TAG... adds tags to the listed entries.

docs.title: Output formats
docs.text:
papers list supports a number of special flags such as --duplicates, --review-required, --broken-file. --format chooses the output:

  • --format line (the default): one line per entry (also -l, -1, --one-liner);
  • --format bibtex: the entries as bibtex (also --plain);
  • --format key: the keys only, one per line (also -K, --key-only), to pipe into other commands (below).

--field FIELD... prints the key and the given fields of each entry (--no-key leaves the key out). -f is a deprecated alias of --field: in v4, -f is no longer --field (it means --force in other commands).

docs.title: Duplicates
docs.text:
papers list --duplicates lists the entries that are the same paper, by the rule of papers add (see Adding entries): the groups that papers check --duplicates would merge or ask about, and not the pairs recorded as distinct in .papers/distinct.json. With --invert, it lists the other entries.

With --fuzzy, it also lists the entries whose authors and title are similar (rapidfuzz token set ratio of at least --fuzzy-ratio, default 80). This is for looking only: papers never merges entries on this score.

With --by key, --by doi or --by title, it lists instead the entries that share that field: the same key (ignoring case), the same DOI, or the same title (ignoring case and punctuation), whether or not they are the same paper by the rule above (--by implies --duplicates).

--duplicates-key, --duplicates-doi and --duplicates-tit are deprecated forms of --duplicates --by key, --by doi and --by title; --similarity is deprecated and has no effect.

docs.title: Naming entries
docs.text:
The commands that act on entries take KEY arguments, where KEY is any of:

  • the key of the entry (case-insensitive), or a former key listed in its biblatex ids field (comma-separated);
  • a DOI: 10.1000/xyz, also written doi:10.1000/xyz or https://doi.org/10.1000/xyz (case-insensitive);
  • an arXiv identifier: 2101.01234, 2101.01234v2, arXiv:2101.01234, or of the old style hep-th/9901001; it matches the eprint field (when archivePrefix is arXiv or absent) and arXiv DOIs (10.48550/arXiv.<id>), whatever the version;
  • an ISBN, 10 or 13 digits, with hyphens or spaces (the ISBN-10 and ISBN-13 forms of a book are the same), matched against the isbn field.

A key cannot start with a digit, so an argument that starts with a digit is never a key. An identifier that matches no entry, or several entries (e.g. an ISBN shared by the chapters of a book), is an error, reported before anything changes.

docs.title: Piping
docs.text:
- reads the identifiers from the standard input, one per line (blank lines are ignored). papers list -K prints the keys of the listed entries, one per line:

papers list smith 2020 -K | papers file rename -
papers list --tag to-read -K | papers open -
papers list --no-file -K | papers check --fetch -
papers list --review-required -K | papers edit -

These commands take -: edit, rm, tag, open, check, and the papers file commands that act on entries (rename, check, and the --key option of detach and rm).

docs.title: Actions on the listed entries
docs.text:
papers list can also act on the entries it lists, as shortcuts of other commands:

  • -e/--edit: edit them in a text editor, as papers edit;
  • --delete: remove them, as papers rm (in a terminal, papers asks whether to delete their files too; --delete-files and --keep-files answer without asking, see Files);
  • --add-tag TAG...: add tags, as papers tag --add.

For instance, the duplicates can be edited by hand with (papers check --duplicates merges them, see Managing your library):

$> papers list --duplicates --edit

The file actions of papers list are deprecated, and print a warning that shows the new form; they will be removed in v4:

Deprecated New form papers list ... --rename (--copy) papers list ... -K \| papers file rename - (--keep-source) papers list ... --add-files FILE... papers file attach KEY FILE... papers list ... -o/--open papers list ... -K \| papers open - papers list ... --fetch papers list ... -K \| papers check --fetch --fetch-all --fix-doi --fix-key --format-name -

docs.title: Libraries and pools
docs.text:
A library is a bibtex file, a files directory and a configuration file (.papersconfig.json), as created by papers init (see Configuration). Each project usually has its own library.

A pool is a library that other libraries exchange entries with. Nothing in the pool marks it as a pool: any library can serve as one, and a pool can be used by several libraries. The pool of a library is its pool setting (a library can also have several pools, see Several pools):

  • by default, the global pool: the pool setting of the global configuration, ~/Documents/papers unless set otherwise (papers config --global pool PATH). A library that uses the global pool stores no path: the same project, copied to another machine, uses the global pool of that machine;
  • a path, set with papers init --pool PATH or papers config pool PATH. A path written relative, or under the library, is stored relative to the library (e.g. ../shared-with-bob); another path is stored as given;
  • none: the library exchanges entries with no pool.

The global pool does not have to exist: papers creates it (as papers init ~/Documents/papers would) the first time it writes to it, and before that a library finds nothing in it, without a warning. A pool given by path that does not exist is a warning (a typo, a disk that is not mounted); papers creates it when it writes to it only if its parent directory exists. The same holds for a global pool outside the home directory (e.g. /media/usb/papers while the disk is not mounted): the command stops before changing anything.

papers init in the folder of the global pool creates the pool itself: a library without pool, with its own files. Outside of any library, commands act on the global pool once it is a library. papers config --global pool none turns sharing off: new libraries get pool: none.

What a library does with its pool:

  • papers add looks in the pool first;
  • papers pull updates the entries shared with the pool, and adds the entries of the pool named, or all of them with --all;
  • papers push updates the entries shared with the pool (those taken from it, or added to it before), and adds the entries named, or all of them with --all;
  • papers sync does both;
  • papers status and papers pull --check tell whether the pool changed since the last exchange with it: up to date, or changed since last pull or push.

Nothing is pulled or pushed automatically, except in libraries that are not local and with the auto-push setting (below): an older project does not change because of work in a newer one.

docs.title: Local or not
docs.text:
The local setting of a library says where its files are:

  • local: false (the default for new libraries): the files are in the files directory of the pool, and the library links to them. A paper used by several projects is stored once;
  • local: true: the files are in the files directory of the library (files/).

papers init --local creates a local library; the default for new libraries is the local setting of the global configuration (papers config --global local true). A library without pool is local.

In a library that is not local:

  • add places new files in the pool's files directory, named with the pool's name template (a name template set on the library is not used), and adds the entry to the pool too (its origin is recorded, see Origin copies); papers file attach and papers file rename do the same with the files they place;
  • pull links to the pool's files instead of copying them;
  • when the pool renames a file, the link breaks: it is repaired by looking the entry up in the pool, when the library is loaded (saved on the next write) and by papers file check --fix.

In any library, rm --delete-files and file rm never delete a file of the pool. Deleting a file in a pool breaks the links of the libraries that use it: it shows up as a broken link there (papers file check). The pool keeps no list of the libraries that depend on it.

A local library with papers config auto-push true also adds the entries new to it to its pool when papers add adds them, as papers push would. Changes to existing entries are never pushed automatically.

docs.title: Sharing a project folder
docs.text:
A project folder shared with coauthors (git, Dropbox...) should be a local library (papers init --local, or papers config local true): the links of a library that is not local point into your own pool, which the others do not have.

A pool can be in a folder synchronized by a cloud client on the local disk (e.g. papers config --global pool ~/Dropbox/papers): papers reads and writes the files there, and the client synchronizes them.

docs.title: Changing local and pool
docs.text:
Changing these settings moves the files of the library. papers lists what it will do and asks Continue? [y/N]; -y answers yes, --dry-run only shows the list, and without a terminal the command stops with the list (pass -y). A file that is not safely in a pool is never deleted, and the files of a pool are never deleted.

Command In a library that is not local In a local library papers config local true the pool files it links to are copied into its files directory (hard links when possible), named with its name template, and the links rewritten; the pool keeps its files nothing to do papers config local false nothing to do the files of its files directory go to the pool: a file that the pool entry of the same paper has (same content) becomes a link to the pool's copy, and the library's copy is deleted; the others are moved into the pool's files directory with the pool's name template and attached to the pool entry; entries that the pool does not have are added to it; the links are rewritten papers config pool none as local true, and the library becomes local the setting changes papers config pool PATH... (or --unset pool: the global pool setting) the files go to the new pool, as with local false; the files of the former pool are copied there (hard links when possible), since other projects may use them the setting changes

With several pools (see Several pools), the files move only when the first pool changes, or when the list becomes empty (pool none). Adding or removing pools further down the list moves nothing. When the first pool changes, the files of the library go to the new first pool, and the files of the pools that leave the list are copied there; files in a pool that stays in the list stay where they are.

Metadata is not merged by these commands: papers push does that.

docs.title: Several pools
docs.text:
The pool setting can list several pools:

papers config pool ~/Documents/papers ../shared-with-bob
papers init --pool ~/Documents/papers --pool ../shared-with-bob
papers config --global pool ~/Documents/papers /media/usb/papers

The configuration file stores one pool as a string and several as a list ("pool": ["~/Documents/papers", "../shared-with-bob"]); none is stored as "none". A library that does not set pool uses the global setting, and stores nothing. The first pool of the global setting is the global pool (origin records name it global, see Origin copies).

The pools are used in order:

  • lookups go through the pools in order, and the first match wins: add (a PDF, --doi, --key, a bibtex entry), pull KEY, and the files of the pools;
  • pull without KEY updates each entry from the pool it came from (its origin copy). pull --all adds the entries of each pool that the library does not have, the pools in order: a paper taken from one pool is not taken again from a later one;
  • writing goes to the first pool only: push, the push of sync, the files of a library that is not local, and the entries that add adds to the pool (also an entry that add took from a later pool);
  • sync pulls from all the pools, then pushes to the first.

--pool PATH on pull, push, sync uses only that pool. papers status and papers init list each pool:

* pools:              ~/Documents/papers (global pool, new entries go here, up to date)
                      ../shared-with-bob (up to date)

A pool of the list that is missing (e.g. a disk that is not mounted) is a warning, and the other pools are still used. An entry that came from the missing pool is not looked up in the others. If the first pool is missing, sync stops with an error before changing anything; push, and add in a library that is not local, create it if its parent directory exists, and otherwise stop with an error, as with a single pool.

docs.title: Keys and identity
docs.text:
The key of an entry belongs to each library: it is what LaTeX documents cite. pull and push never change the key of an entry that the library they write to has. An entry new to the pool gets a key from the pool's key template; an entry of the pool new to the library keeps the pool key, with a letter suffix if the library has that key already (Smith_2020b).

A library entry and a pool entry are matched by the same rule as duplicates (see Same paper): same DOI, arXiv identifier, ISBN (two books), or else the same authors and title. The pairs recorded as "not the same paper" (.papers/distinct.json) are merged both ways on pull and push.

docs.title: Origin copies
docs.text:
.papers/origin.bib, next to the bibtex of the library, records for each entry exchanged with a pool (by add, pull or push) its origin copy, under the library's key, with the pool (papers-pool: global for the global pool, otherwise the path of the pool relative to the library), the key in the pool (papers-pool-key) and the time (papers-time). It also records the modification time of the pool's bibtex at the last exchange with the pool: a pull of all entries that skipped no conflict, or a push or an add when the pool had not changed since the previous exchange (or when it is the first exchange). A push that leaves the pool entry with fields or files that the library entry does not have does not count: papers status then shows the pool as changed until the next pull. The file is part of the git backup of the library (see Git integration).

The origin copy is the third version of a three-way merge: comparing the library entry and the pool entry with it tells which side changed a field. It is the version of the side that sent the entry, as it was sent: the pool entry after add and pull, the library entry after push. What the receiving side has beyond it is a change of that side, for the next exchange the other way: a field that only the pool entry has comes with the next pull; a field that only the library entry has goes to the pool with the next push.

papers add other.bib copies the entries of other.bib once, and keeps no memory of where they came from. The entries taken with papers pull stay linked to the pool through their origin copy: later pulls bring the corrections made in the pool.

docs.title: add looks in the pool first
docs.text:
When the paper added is already in the pool, papers add takes the pool's entry, without querying crossref:

  • a PDF with the same content as a file of a pool entry, or whose DOI (from the PDF metadata, or a DOI of its text whose title in the pool appears in the text) is in the pool;
  • a DOI (papers add --doi DOI) that a pool entry has;
  • a key (papers add --key KEY, with no file, DOI or other field) that a pool entry has, ignoring case: the entry keeps the pool key. Without such an entry (and without a library entry of that key), add stops with an error;
  • an entry of an added bibtex that is the same paper as a pool entry: the pool's fields are taken, the entry keeps its key, and its fields that the pool entry does not have are kept.

The entry gets the pool's files: in a local library in copy and move mode they are copied into the library's files directory (a hard link when possible), named with the library's name template; a pool file is never moved. In link mode, and in a library that is not local, the entry links to the pool's file. A PDF given that has the same content as a file of the pool entry is removed in move mode, since it is stored already, and kept in copy and link mode; a PDF with other content is attached to the entry as another file, placed as the files mode says. The origin copy is recorded. --no-pool skips the lookup.

docs.title: papers pull
docs.text:
papers pull [KEY...|-] [--all] [--pool PATH] [--on-duplicate MODE] [--check]

Without KEY, pull updates the entries shared with the pool: those with an origin copy, each from the pool it came from. For each of them (or each entry named, or every entry with --all), papers finds its pool entry (by its origin copy, else by the same-paper rule) and merges it into the library entry, field by field:

Field changed since the origin copy Result in the pool only taken from the pool (+ in the dialogue) in the library only (e.g. a field adapted to a journal style) kept, without asking on both sides, to different values a conflict (!)

A field removed on one side keeps the other side's state: removed in the pool, it stays in the library; removed in the library, it does not come back. File links are merged: new files of the pool entry are linked in a library that is not local, and otherwise copied into the library's files directory as the files setting says. The key of the library entry never changes. After the merge, the origin copy is the pool's current version. A skipped conflict leaves the pool shown as changed in papers status.

An entry without origin copy (added before the pool was used, or with --no-pool) is not shared: pull without KEY leaves it alone. Named on the command line, or with --all, it is matched to the pool by the same-paper rule. Its differences with the pool entry are conflicts (there is no origin to tell which side changed), and the origin copy is recorded afterwards ("linked").

An entry that the pool does not have is reported (Not found) only when it is named on the command line. Without KEY, it is left as it is.

A KEY is looked up in the library first, then in the pool (its key, DOI, arXiv identifier or ISBN): an entry of the pool that the library does not have is added to it, with its origin copy (added), under the pool key (see Keys and identity); its files are linked in a library that is not local, otherwise copied as the files setting says (a hard link when possible). An identifier found in neither is an error, and nothing is changed. --all adds every entry of the pool that the library does not have (same-paper rule). Without KEY or --all, pull only updates the entries shared with the pool, like push and sync. A pool that does not exist or is not a library is an error of pull, pull --check and sync, and nothing is changed (the global pool that was not created yet is not: there is nothing to pull).

--pool PATH pulls from another pool, once: the origin copies record that pool.

pull prints one line per entry added (Added ->), modified (Modified ->), left with a conflict (Conflict ->) or, among the entries named, not found in the pool (Not found ->), with the pool in brackets, then the counts when more than one entry was involved: added, modified, skipped, not found, unchanged, and linked (an entry without origin copy, the same as its pool entry: its origin copy is recorded). push prints the same lines for the pool entries. When add (or file attach) also adds or changes the entry in the pool, or takes it from the pool, its line says so in brackets: [also added to pool ~/Documents/papers], [from pool ~/Documents/papers].

Conflicts are decided as for duplicates (see The dialogue), with --on-duplicate:

Mode Conflicts ask (default in a terminal) the dialogue: 1 keeps the library values, 2 takes the pool values, f goes field by field (also through the changes from the pool), e edits, s skips, q quits keep the library values are kept update the pool values are taken skip the entry is not changed, and its origin copy is not updated: it comes again next time error (default without a terminal) stop before saving anything

Fields changed in the pool only need no decision: they are taken in every mode.

papers pull --check only reports: whether the pool changed since the last pull (a modification time check), and the entries whose pool version changed since their origin copy, with the fields (without KEY, the entries shared with the pool). papers status shows the first part too.

docs.title: papers push
docs.text:
papers push [KEY...|-] [--all] [--pool PATH] [--on-duplicate MODE]

The reverse of pull, into the pool of the library (or --pool PATH, once). Without KEY, only the entries shared with the pool are pushed: those with an origin copy from it (taken from it by add or pull, or pushed to it before). push KEY... pushes the entries named, and push --all every entry of the library:

  • an entry that is not in the pool is added to it, with a key from the pool's key template; its files are copied into the pool's files directory (a hard link when possible), named with the pool's name template;
  • an entry that is in the pool is merged three-way into the pool entry: fields changed in the library only are taken, fields changed in the pool only are kept, conflicts are decided with --on-duplicate (keep: the pool values, update: the library values). The pool key does not change.

Push does not change the library: after it, the origin copy is the library version that was pushed, and the fields that only the pool entry has come with the next pull (or papers sync). The pool is created if it does not exist yet.

docs.title: papers sync
docs.text:
papers sync [KEY...|-] [--all] [--pool PATH] [--on-duplicate MODE]

runs papers pull, then papers push of the same entries:

  • without KEY, the entries shared with the pool (with an origin copy from it). An entry added to the library with --no-pool, or before the pool was used, is not exchanged: name it, or use --all;
  • with KEY..., the entries named. A KEY that only the pool has is added to the library, as with pull, and a KEY that only the library has is added to the pool, as with push;
  • with --all, pull --all then push --all: each side gets the entries it does not have.

If the pull leaves conflicts undecided (skipped, or the dialogue quit), nothing is pushed: decide them with papers pull, then sync again. When nothing changed, sync prints one line:

$ papers sync
nothing to sync with pool ~/Documents/papers (2 entries unchanged)

With --pool PATH, sync reads and writes only the library at PATH, not the pool of the library. Without KEY, it exchanges the entries shared with that library only, so the first time nothing is exchanged:

$ papers sync --pool ../shared-with-bob
nothing to sync with pool ../shared-with-bob: no entries shared with it (`papers sync --all` adds the entries missing on each side)
The entries taken from it link to its files in a library that is not local (in a local library, they are copied as the files setting says), and the entries pushed to it get copies of their files in its files directory.

docs.title: Undo in a pool
docs.text: A pool is a library with its own backup history (see Git integration). papers undo in a library undoes a change of that library only: an entry that add also added to the pool stays in the pool. To undo a change in the pool, run the command in the pool, e.g. papers -C ~/Documents/papers undo for the global pool.

docs.title: papers export
docs.text:
papers export DIR [KEY...|-] [--files copy|link|none]

writes the entries (all without KEY) as a new library in DIR, which must not exist or be empty, to hand over: its bibtex, its files directory, and its configuration (with the name and key templates that the library sets, local: true and pool: none). File links are relative to the new bibtex.

  • --files copy (default) copies the files into DIR/files (hard links when possible), named with the name template;
  • --files link links to the files where they are;
  • --files none leaves the file links out.

papers add DIR --recursive adds an exported library to another one, and papers config pool DIR makes it the pool of the library.

docs.title: A shared files folder without a pool
docs.text:
In papers 2, several libraries could keep their PDFs in one folder: each library has its own bibtex, no pool (pool: none), its own files (local: true), and a filesdir that points to a common folder outside the project, e.g. ~/Documents/papers/sealevel used by two projects. This setup still works in v3.

It is less efficient than a pool. Each library has its own bibtex, and knows nothing of the others: adding to the second library a paper that the first one has (even its PDF, already in the shared folder) reads the PDF again, extracts its DOI and fetches the entry from crossref (the request is answered from the cache when the same DOI was fetched on this machine). Changes to an entry in one library do not reach the other.

The pool model of v3 avoids this: by default, a library is not local (it has no files of its own) and its entries are copies of the entries of the pool, whose PDFs are in the pool's files folder. A paper that is in the pool already is taken from it, without reading the PDF or fetching anything, and papers sync keeps the copies up to date. In both setups, each PDF is stored once.

A shared files folder without a pool is enough when the libraries are independent, and you do not want a central bibliography. To set it up:

papers init --pool none --filesdir ~/Documents/papers/sealevel   # local, since it has no pool
papers config pool none                                          # in an existing library
papers config filesdir ~/Documents/papers/sealevel               # the shared folder
papers config --global pool none   # no pool for the libraries that do not set one, new ones included

A library configuration of papers 2 without pool setting is read as a local library (its files are its own) that uses the global pool. It looks entries up in the global pool if that exists, but writes nothing to it: add in a local library adds new entries to the pool only with auto-push, and push and sync without KEY exchange only the entries shared with the pool. papers config pool none stops the lookups.

What to watch for, since each library only knows its own entries:

  • papers file clean in one library lists the PDFs of the other libraries in the shared folder as unlinked, and deletes them once confirmed (or with -y). Use --dry-run to see the list.
  • papers rm --delete-files and papers file rm keep a PDF that another entry of the same library links to, but not one that another library links to.
  • papers file rename in one library renames the shared PDF, and the link of the other library breaks. papers file check reports the broken link there, and --fix does not repair it (the repair of broken links only covers the files of a pool): remove the link with papers file detach --broken --key KEY, and attach the renamed file with papers file attach KEY FILE.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The global pool in ~/Documents/papers, and two projects:

mkdir -p ~/projects/sealevel ~/projects/tides
cd ~/projects/sealevel
papers init                               # the global pool, not local
papers add ~/Downloads/esd-4-11-2013.pdf  # fetched from crossref; the PDF goes to
                                          # ~/Documents/papers/files, the entry to both

cd ~/projects/tides
papers init
papers add --doi 10.5194/esd-4-11-2013    # taken from the pool: no query, the file is linked

Later, the entry is completed in the pool (e.g. its pages), and adapted in tides (a journal abbreviation):

cd ~/projects/tides
papers status                  # pool: ~/Documents/papers (global pool, changed since last pull or push)
papers pull --check            # perrette_landerer2013: changed in pool ~/Documents/papers: pages
papers pull                    # pages taken; the journal abbreviation is kept

A project shared with a colleague through git keeps its own files:

cd ~/projects/sealevel
papers config local true       # copies the pool files into files/ (hard links), after asking

A folder shared with someone as a separate pool, for one project:

cd ~/projects/tides
papers export ../shared-with-bob          # a library of its own
papers config pool ../shared-with-bob     # the pool of tides from now on
papers sync --all                         # the first time: records what is shared
papers sync                               # later changes, both ways

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
papers works like git: one command with subcommands, run inside a folder that holds a library. A library is a bibtex file and a small configuration file, .papersconfig.json. By default the PDFs of all your libraries are kept in one folder, ~/Documents/papers, called the pool, so that a paper used in several projects is stored once.

The examples below use two papers of the Copernicus journals, whose PDFs contain their DOI: papers reads the DOI from the PDF and fetches the bibtex entry from crossref.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install --pre papers-cli

--pre installs the 3.0 beta. Python 3.11 or later is needed. See Installation for other ways to install.

docs.title: Create a library
docs.text:
Run papers init in the folder of your project:

$ cd ~/projects/sea-level
$ papers init
created the library ~/projects/sea-level
* bibtex:  papers.bib
* files:   in the pool ~/Documents/papers
* backup:  git
`papers status -v` shows all settings

Commands run in this folder, or below it, use this library.

docs.title: Add papers
docs.text:
Add a PDF. It is moved to the pool and renamed after the entry, and the entry is added to the bibtex of the project and to the pool's own bibtex (the pool is created the first time):

$ papers add ~/Downloads/esd-4-11-2013.pdf
Added -> perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1) [also added to pool ~/Documents/papers]
$ ls ~/Documents/papers/files
perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise-and-its-uncertainties.pdf
$ grep "file =" papers.bib
 file = {:../../Documents/papers/files/perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise-and-its-uncertainties.pdf:pdf},

Add an entry from its DOI, without a PDF:

$ papers add --doi 10.5194/bg-8-515-2011
Added -> perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011) [also added to pool ~/Documents/papers]

Attach another file to an entry, such as a supplement. It is named after the entry, with its original name as a label:

$ papers file attach perrette_landerer2013 ~/Downloads/esd-4-11-2013-supplement.pdf
Modified -> perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, files:2) [also modified in pool ~/Documents/papers]
$ ls ~/Documents/papers/files
perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise-and-its-uncertainties--esd-4-11-2013-supplement.pdf
perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise-and-its-uncertainties.pdf

add also takes a bibtex file (papers add refs.bib), a folder of PDFs (papers add -R ~/Downloads/papers/), or fields given by hand. See Adding entries and Files.

docs.title: List and search
docs.text:
$ papers list
perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, files:2)
perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011)
$ papers list -a yool
perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011)

papers list --format bibtex prints the entries as bibtex, and papers list -K prints their keys only, to pass them to another command (papers list -a yool -K | papers file rename -). See Listing and searching.

docs.title: Undo
docs.text:
Every change to the bibtex is recorded in a git repository of its own, so papers undo takes back the last change of the library (when git is installed), and papers redo restores it:

$ papers undo
undo: papers.bib restored to 7f9ad3e papers add --doi 10.5194/bg-8-515-2011 (2026-10-22 15:37)
$ papers redo
redo: papers.bib restored to 55b0a37 papers file attach perrette_landerer2013 /home/you/Downloads/esd-4-11-2013-supplement.pdf (2026-10-22 15:37)

The pool is a library with its own git history: papers undo in a project undoes only the project, and papers -C ~/Documents/papers undo undoes a change in the pool. See Undo and redo and Undo in a pool.

docs.title: A second project
docs.text:
In another project, add --doi or add --key finds a paper that is already in the pool: nothing is fetched online, and the PDF is not stored twice.

$ cd ~/projects/new-paper
$ papers init
$ papers add --doi 10.5194/esd-4-11-2013
Added -> perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, files:2) [from pool ~/Documents/papers]
$ papers add --key perrette_yool2011
Added -> perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011) [from pool ~/Documents/papers]

The pool is an ordinary library: papers -C ~/Documents/papers list lists all your papers.

docs.title: Keep libraries in sync
docs.text:
The entries taken from the pool, or added to it, stay linked to it: they are shared with it. papers sync sends the changes of the shared entries to the pool and brings the changes of the pool into the library. A tag added in the first project reaches the second one:

$ cd ~/projects/sea-level
$ papers tag perrette_yool2011 --add arctic
Modified -> perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011, arctic)
$ papers sync
pull from pool ~/Documents/papers: 2 unchanged
Modified -> perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011, arctic) [in pool ~/Documents/papers]
push to pool ~/Documents/papers: 1 unchanged, 1 modified

$ cd ~/projects/new-paper
$ papers sync
Modified -> perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011, arctic) [from pool ~/Documents/papers]
pull from pool ~/Documents/papers: 1 unchanged, 1 modified
push to pool ~/Documents/papers: 2 unchanged
$ papers sync
nothing to sync with pool ~/Documents/papers (2 entries unchanged)

papers sync --pool PATH syncs with another library instead, such as a folder shared with a coauthor. It reads and writes only that library, not the global pool. A KEY that only that library has is added, and the entry links to the PDF of that library (in a library that is not local, as here):

$ papers sync --pool ../shared-with-bob agnew_farrell1978
Added -> agnew_farrell1978: Self-consistent equilibrium ocean tides (file:1) [from pool ../shared-with-bob]
push to pool ../shared-with-bob: 1 unchanged

Without KEY, only the entries shared with that library are exchanged; papers sync --all exchanges everything: each side gets the entries it does not have, with copies of their PDFs.

Nothing is exchanged without these commands, except that add adds new papers to the pool. Each library keeps its own keys. papers pull and papers push do each half of sync, and papers status tells whether the pool changed since the last exchange: see Pools.

docs.title: Where the PDFs are
docs.text: By default the PDFs of all your libraries are in the pool, ~/Documents/papers, and the bibtex of each library links to them there (papers config --global pool PATH moves the default pool elsewhere). A project folder shared with others (git, Dropbox) should keep its own PDFs, in its files/ folder: create it with papers init --local, or run papers config local true in an existing library, which copies its PDFs from the pool (as hard links when possible). A local library still uses the pool for entries. papers init --pool none creates a library without pool: its PDFs are in the project, and nothing is shared. A library can also have several pools, looked up in order (see Several pools), and several libraries without a pool can share one PDF folder, as in papers 2 (see A shared files folder without a pool). See Pools in the configuration, and Local or not and Changing local and pool in the Pools guide.

docs.title: Entries with several files
docs.text:
The first file of an entry (the PDF) is named after the name template, and any other file (attachments, e.g. supplementary material added with --attach or papers file attach) is placed next to it, under the same name followed by -- and the file's original name:

files/perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach.pdf
files/perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach--esd-4-11-2013-supplement.pdf

The label after -- is kept when the entry is renamed again (e.g. after its title or year was fixed), so only the part before -- changes. If two attachments have the same original name, the second one gets a -2 suffix.

Versions before 2.19 placed the files of an entry with several files in a folder named after the entry, with a hidden copy of the entry (files/<name>/.<name>.bib). Such folders keep working as they are: their files are linked from the bibtex, and nothing is moved until the entry is renamed. Renaming (papers file rename) moves the files out of the folder into the layout above, and removes the folder if nothing but the hidden bibtex is left in it (a folder with other files is kept, and the files left in it are reported).

docs.title: Renaming the files of existing entries
docs.text:
papers add places new files in the files directory under their template name (unless the files setting is link, see Files). To rename the files of entries already in the library, e.g. after changing the name template or fixing an entry's title:

papers file rename                      # all entries
papers file rename perrette2013         # some entries
papers list --year 2013 -K | papers file rename -

Each file is moved into the files directory under its new name; --keep-source keeps the original too (a hard link when possible). A file that belongs to another library is copied, not moved. The deprecated papers filecheck --rename and papers list ... --rename run this command.

docs.title: Control fields when renaming files
docs.text:
$> papers add --move --info --name-template "{AuthorX}{year}-{Title}" --name-title-sep '' --name-author-sep '' esd-4-11-2013
INFO:papers:found doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013
INFO:papers:new entry: perrette2013scaling
INFO:papers:create directory: files/2013

docs.title: Case-sensitive fields
docs.text:
Entries are case-sensitive, and a few more fields are added, so that:

  • author generates perrette
  • Author generates Perrette
  • AUTHOR generates PERRETTE
  • authorX generates perrette, perrette_and_landerer or perrette_et_al depending on the number of authors
  • AuthorX same as authorX but capitalized

docs.title: Modifiers
docs.text:
The modifiers are:

  • --name-title-sep: separator for title words
  • --name-title-length: max title length, with its separators: the last words are dropped until the title fits, and a first word longer than that is cut
  • --name-title-word-size: min size to be considered a word
  • --name-title-word-num: max number of title words

and similarly:

  • --name-author-sep: separator for authors
  • --name-author-num: number of authors (not relevant for {authorX})

and for entries without author, year or title:

  • --name-unknown-template: the template used instead (default: unknown_{doi_or_id} for file names, {doi_} for keys)
  • --name-unknown-strict: use it only when author, year and title are all missing (by default, when any of them is missing); --no-name-unknown-strict turns off the name.unknown-strict setting for one command

The same template and modifiers system applies to the bibtex key generation by replacing the prefix --name- with --key-, e.g. --key-template.

In the common case where the bibtex (--bibtex), files directory (--filesdir), and name and key formats (e.g. --name-template) do not change, it is convenient to store them in a library configuration (papers init, papers config name.template ...).

docs.title: Undo and redo
docs.text:
Did a papers add and are unhappy with the result?

papers undo

will revert to the previous version. Without git-tracking, repeating it only jumps back and forth between the latest and before-latest version.

With git-tracking (the default for fresh installs), papers undo and papers redo step through the whole history of the library (-n N steps at once). History is append-only: undo and redo record restore commits in the backup repository instead of rewriting it, so no state is ever lost. In particular, making a new change while undone starts a new line of history on top, and the states that were still redoable remain reachable with further papers undo or with papers restore --ref COMMIT (use papers git log to find COMMIT). papers restore without --ref restores the last version of the backup. papers restore-backup is the deprecated name of papers restore.

papers undo and papers redo print the state they restore, with the command that made it, e.g.

undo: papers.bib restored to 3f2a1c9 papers add paper.pdf (2026-10-22 14:03)

Files that the undone command placed in the files directory stay there. When no entry links to them any more (e.g. after undoing papers file attach), papers lists them: papers file clean removes them.

See Git integration for how to enable git-tracking.
